content: Engaging in regular physical activity is recommended for substantial health benefits. This includes either 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise, or a combination of both intensities spread throughout the week. This recommendation is particularly relevant for reducing anxiety symptoms in adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) or panic disorder. In resource-limited settings, physical exercise may be a more feasible option compared to intensive psychological interventions. The type of exercise should be tailored to individual preferences and practical considerations. For individuals with moderate-to-severe anxiety disorders, exercise is best used as an adjunct to pharmacological and/or psychological treatments. Research Gaps in Physical Activity for Anxiety The types of physical exercises studied in reviews vary significantly. Further research with standardized intervention formats, including clear descriptions of exercise type, duration, and intensity, is needed to establish best practices. Implementation Considerations for Physical Activity Cultural differences in the perceived value of exercise may influence its adoption and success. This intervention may be less suitable for individuals with physically demanding lifestyles and more relevant for those with sedentary habits. Benzodiazepines for Anxiety Disorders Benzodiazepines are not recommended for the treatment of adults with GAD or panic disorder. They may be considered for short-term (3–7 days maximum) emergency management of acute and severe anxiety symptoms. Evidence suggests that while benzodiazepines can reduce anxiety and improve functioning, they also carry risks of adverse effects, dependence, and treatment dropout. The risks outweigh the benefits, leading to a strong recommendation against their routine use. Remarks on Benzodiazepines Benzodiazepines studied for panic disorder include alprazolam, clonazepam, diazepam, and midazolam. Specific data on their use for GAD were not reported. Long-term use beyond the recommended period requires monitoring by trained specialists and is outside the scope of these guidelines. Research Gaps Most studies on benzodiazepines have been conducted in high-income countries (HICs), with limited data on their use in low-resource settings. There is also a lack of studies on the long-term safety and effectiveness of benzodiazepines. Implementation Considerations Benzodiazepines should only be prescribed in select cases of acute and severe anxiety where other treatments have failed or are unavailable. Patients should be informed about treatment options, expected symptom improvement timelines, and the potential for addiction. Gradual discontinuation is advised once symptoms improve to avoid tolerance. For individuals showing signs of dependence, withdrawal management strategies should be considered. Collaborative Care for Depression and Anxiety Collaborative care (CC) is recommended for adults with depression and/or anxiety, particularly those with coexisting physical health conditions. This model involves a multidisciplinary team, including a care manager, and emphasizes coordinated mental health and medical care. Evidence suggests that CC reduces depression and anxiety symptoms and improves physical health outcomes. Remarks on Collaborative Care CC typically involves systematic screening, evidence-based interventions, medication administration (if needed), and regular monitoring of mental health symptoms. The model is resource-intensive but feasible in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) with appropriate resource allocation. Research Gaps Further research is needed to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of CC in LMICs and to identify the most effective components of the model. Implementation Considerations CC requires significant human resources and training for medical teams and mental health providers. ADHD in Children and Adolescents For children aged six years and older with ADHD, methylphenidate may be considered if symptoms cause significant impairment despite environmental modifications. Prescriptions should be made by or in consultation with a specialist. Methylphenidate has shown substantial effects on symptom reduction but requires close clinical monitoring due to potential side effects, such as weight loss. Remarks on Methylphenidate Treatment should be part of a comprehensive management plan addressing psychosocial risks and environmental factors. Combining methylphenidate with brief parent behavioral therapies is recommended. Regular reassessment of the management plan by a specialist is essential. Research Gaps There is limited evidence on the long-term efficacy and safety of methylphenidate beyond 12 weeks. Further studies are needed to evaluate lasting intervention effects and treatment satisfaction. Psychosocial Interventions for Children Universal psychosocial interventions, such as curriculum-based, family-based, or exercise-based methods, should be considered to promote emotional regulation and psychosocial well-being in children. School-based interventions are particularly promising for delivering these programs at scale. Remarks on Psychosocial Interventions Emotional regulation is a critical domain for broader psychosocial well-being. Interventions often include social and personal skills development and behavior management strategies. Research Gaps More rigorous studies with long-term follow-up are needed to evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions, particularly for reducing emotional problems and preventing mental health diagnoses. Implementation Considerations Efforts should be made to reach vulnerable children, including those with disabilities or out of school, and to address psychosocial risks and environmental determinants of mental health. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Psychosocial interventions focusing on social skills training and developmental behavioral approaches are recommended to improve development, well-being, and functioning in children and adolescents with autism. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is also effective for reducing anxiety in individuals with autism who have the verbal and cognitive ability to engage in therapy. Remarks on Interventions for Autism Social skills training involves teaching appropriate behaviors in everyday situations and can be delivered in various formats, including peer-mediated and group-based interventions. Adjustments to interventions, such as using visual supports and involving caregivers, may be necessary to meet the needs of individuals with autism. Research Gaps Further research is needed to identify the most effective components of social skills training and to address gaps in knowledge about interventions for females with autism and individuals with lower-functioning autism. Implementation Considerations Interventions should be implemented within broader strategies promoting inclusive environments. ADHD Psychosocial Interventions Psychosocial interventions focusing on social, cognitive, and organizational skills training should be considered for children and adolescents with ADHD. These interventions improve functional outcomes, including attention, behavior, and school performance. Remarks on ADHD Interventions Social skills training typically involves role play, exercises, and group sessions lasting 8–12 weeks. Organizational skills training focuses on managing materials, time, and tasks through structured learning activities. Implementation Considerations Both individual and group-based formats can be adapted to meet the needs of children and adolescents. Interventions should be part of broader strategies promoting inclusive environments and access to health and social care services.
